source_text: Θυσία δὲ ἡ τῷ θεῷ δεκτὴ σώματός τε καὶ τῶν τούτου παθῶν ἀμετανόητος χωρισμός. ἡ ἀληθὴς τῷ ὄντι θεοσέβεια αὕτη. καὶ μή τι εἰκότως μελέτη θανάτου διὰ τοῦτο εἴρηται τῷ Σωκράτει ἡ φιλοσοφία· ὁ γὰρ μήτε τὴν ὄψιν παρατιθέμενος ἐν τῷ διανοεῖσθαι μήτε τινὰ τῶν ἄλλων αἰσθήσεων ἐφελκόμενος, ἀλλ’ αὐτῷ καθαρῷ τῷ νῷ τοῖς πράγμασιν ἐντυγχάνων τὴν ἀληθῆ φιλοσοφίαν μέτεισιν. τοῦτο ἄρα βούλεται καὶ τῷ Πυθαγόρᾳ ἡ τῆς πενταετίας σιωπή, ἣν τοῖς γνωρίμοις παρεγγυᾷ, ὡς δὴ ἀποστραφέντες τῶν αἰσθητῶν ψιλῷ τῷ νῷ τὸ θεῖον ἐποπτεύοιεν. παρὰ Μωυσέως τοιαῦτα φιλοσοφήσαντες οἱ τῶν Ἑλλήνων ἄκροι. προστάσσει γὰρ τὰ ὁλοκαυτώματα δείραντας εἰς μέλη διανεῖμαι, ἐπειδὴ γυμνὴν τῆς ὑλικῆς δορᾶς γενομένην τὴν γνωστικὴν ψυχὴν ἄνευ τῆς σωματικῆς φλυαρίας καὶ τῶν παθῶν πάντων, ὅσα περιποιοῦσιν αἱ κεναὶ καὶ ψευδεῖς ὑπολήψεις, ἀποδυσαμένην τὰς σαρκικὰς ἐπιθυμίας, τῷ φωτὶ καθιερωθῆναι ἀνάγκη. οἱ δὲ πλεῖστοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων τὸ θνητὸν ἐνδυόμενοι καθάπερ οἱ κοχλίαι καὶ περὶ τὰς αὑτῶν ἀκρασίας ὥσπερ οἱ ἐχῖνοι σφαιρηδὸν εἱλούμενοι περὶ τοῦ μακαρίου καὶ ἀφθάρτου θεοῦ τοιαῦτα οἷα καὶ περὶ αὑτῶν δοξάζουσιν. λέληθεν δ’ αὐτούς, κἂν πλησίον ἡμῶν τύχωσιν, ὡς μυρία ὅσα δεδώρηται ἡμῖν ὁ θεός, ὧν αὐτὸς ἀμέτοχος, γένεσιν μὲν ἀγένητος ὤν, τροφὴν δὲ ἀνενδεὴς ὤν, καὶ αὔξησιν ἐν ἰσότητι ὤν, εὐγηρίαν τε καὶ εὐθανασίαν ἀθάνατός τε καὶ ἀγήρως ὑπάρχων. διὸ καὶ χεῖρας καὶ πόδας καὶ στόμα καὶ ὀφθαλμοὺς καὶ εἰσόδους καὶ ἐξόδους καὶ ὀργὰς καὶ ἀπειλὰς μὴ πάθη θεοῦ τις ὑπολάβῃ παρὰ Ἑβραίοις λέγεσθαι, μηδαμῶς, ἀλληγορεῖσθαι δέ τινα ἐκ τούτων τῶν ὀνομάτων ὁσιώτερον, ἃ δὴ καὶ προϊόντος τοῦ λόγου κατὰ τὸν οἰκεῖον καιρὸν διασαφήσομεν. ἦ πανακὲς πάντων φάρμακον ἁ σοφία, Καλλίμαχος ἐν τοῖς ἐπιγράμμασι γράφει· ἕτερος (δὲ) ἐξ ἑτέρου σοφὸς τό τε πάλαι τό τε νῦν, φησὶ Βακχυλίδης ἐν τοῖς Παιᾶσιν· οὐδὲ γὰρ ῥᾷστον ἀρρήτων ἐπέων πύλας ἐξευρεῖν· καλῶς ἄρα Ἰσοκράτης ἐν τῷ Παναθηναϊκῷ τίνας οὖν καλῶ πεπαιδευμένους; προθεὶς ἐπιφέρει· πρῶτον μὲν τοὺς καλῶς χρωμένους τοῖς πράγμασι τοῖς κατὰ τὴν ἡμέραν ἑκάστην προσπίπτουσι καὶ τὴν δόξαν ἐπιτυχῆ τῶν καιρῶν ἔχοντας καὶ δυναμένην ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πολὺ στοχάζεσθαι τοῦ συμφέροντος· ἔπειτα τοὺς πρεπόντως καὶ δικαίως ὁμιλοῦντας ἀεὶ τοῖς πλησιάζουσι καὶ τὰς μὲν τῶν ἄλλων ἀηδίας καὶ βαρύτητας εὐκόλως καὶ ῥᾳδίως φέροντας, σφᾶς δ’ αὐτοὺς ὡς δυνατὸν ἐλαφροτάτους καὶ μετριωτάτους τοῖς ξυνοῦσι παρέχοντας· ἔτι δὲ τοὺς τῶν μὲν ἡδονῶν κρατοῦντας, τῶν δὲ συμφορῶν μὴ λίαν ἡττωμένους, ἀλλ’ ἀνδρωδῶς ἐν αὐταῖς ἀναστρεφομένους καὶ τῆς φύσεως ἀξίως ἧς μετέχοντες τυγχάνομεν· τέταρτον, ὅπερ μέγιστόν ἐστι, τοὺς μὴ διαφθειρομένους ὑπὸ τῶν εὐπραγιῶν μηδ’ ἐξισταμένους αὑτῶν μηδὲ ὑπερηφάνους γινομένους, ἀλλ’ ἐμμένοντας τῇ τάξει τῶν εὖ φρονούντων. εἶτα ἐπιφέρει τὸν κολοφῶνα τοῦ λόγου· τοὺς δὲ μὴ μόνον πρὸς ἓν τούτων, ἀλλὰ πρὸς ἅπαντα ταῦτα τὴν ἕξιν τῆς ψυχῆς εὐάρμοστον ἔχοντας, τούτους φημὶ καὶ φρονίμους εἶναι καὶ τελείους ἄνδρας καὶ πάσας ἔχειν τὰς ἀρετάς.
pass_a_gloss: The sacrifice acceptable to God is the unregretted separation from the body and its passions. This is true devotion to the existing God. And it is not without reason that the study of death is called philosophy by Socrates, for he who neither presents sight in his thinking nor is drawn in by any of the other senses, but encounters things with his pure mind, pursues true philosophy. This is also what Pythagoras means by the five-year silence, which he prescribes to those who know him, so that, turning away from sensory things, they may contemplate the divine with a pure mind. The greatest of the Greeks have philosophized in this way, following Moses, who commands that the whole burnt offerings be cut into parts and distributed, since the soul that has become naked, having shed the bodily flesh and all passions, which are caused by empty and false assumptions, and having stripped off fleshly desires, must be dedicated to the light. Most people, however, put on mortality like snails and are wrapped around their own excesses like hedgehogs, and they think such things about the blessed and immortal God as they do about themselves. It has escaped their notice, even if they are near us, that God has given us countless things, of which He Himself is without need, being unborn, unneeding, equal, and immortal, and having a good old age and a good death. Therefore, no one should think that hands, feet, mouth, eyes, entrances, exits, organs, and threats are passions of God, as is said among the Hebrews, but rather that some of these names are allegorized in a more holy way, which we will clarify as the discussion proceeds. Wisdom is the panacea of all things, as Callimachus writes in his epigrams. Another wise man says, 'One becomes wise from another, both in the past and in the present,' as Bacchylides says in his Paens. For it is not easy to find the gates of unspoken words. Isocrates says in his Panathenaic Oration, 'What kind of people do I call educated?' He answers, 'First, those who use things well in their daily lives and have a good reputation in their times and are able to think about what is beneficial for the most part. Then, those who converse with their neighbors in a fitting and just manner, bearing the unpleasantness and heaviness of others easily and lightly, and offering themselves as lightly and moderately as possible to those who are with them. Furthermore, those who master their pleasures and are not overly defeated by their misfortunes, but behave like men in them and live worthily of the nature they share. Fourth, and most importantly, those who are not corrupted by their good fortune, nor do they become conceited or proud, but remain steadfast in the order of those who think well.' Then he concludes his discussion, 'But I say that those who have a soul that is well-ordered in all these respects are wise and perfect men and have all the virtues.'

choices.why: The Greek word ἀμετανόητος means 'unregretted' or 'without regret'.
The Greek word ὁλοκαυτώματα refers to 'whole burnt offerings' in a sacrificial context.
The Greek word γνωστικὴν refers to 'gnostic' or 'related to knowledge'.

pass_b_english: The sacrifice acceptable to God is the unregretted separation of soul from body and its passions, and this constitutes true devotion to the living God. It is therefore not without reason that Socrates calls philosophy a study of death; for the philosopher neither brings sight into his thinking nor allows himself to be drawn by any other sense, but encounters reality with a pure mind and so pursues true philosophy. Pythagoras intends the same thing by the five-year silence he prescribes to his acquaintances, so that, turning away from sensory things, they may contemplate the divine with a bare intellect. The greatest of the Greeks have philosophized in this manner, following Moses; for he commands that the whole burnt offerings be flayed and divided into parts (Leviticus 1:9), since the cognitive soul, once stripped naked of its material covering and having shed all passions born of empty and false assumptions and stripped off fleshly desires, must be dedicated to the light. Most people, however, clothe themselves in mortality like snails and curl around their own excesses like hedgehogs, and they attribute to the blessed and immortal God the very qualities they find in themselves. This escapes their notice, even when they are near us: God has given us countless gifts of which He Himself has no share—being unborn, He has no need of birth; being self-sufficient, He has no need of nourishment; being unchanging, He has no need of growth; being immortal and ageless, He has no need of a good old age or a good death. Therefore no one should suppose that hands, feet, mouth, eyes, entrances, exits, organs, and threats are passions of God, as they are spoken of among the Hebrews; rather, certain of these names are to be understood allegorically in a holier sense, which we will clarify as the discussion proceeds. Wisdom is the panacea for all things, as Callimachus writes in his epigrams, and Bacchylides says in his Paeans, 'One man becomes wise from another, both in the past and in the present.' For it is not easy to find the gates of unspoken words. Isocrates asks in his Panathenaic Oration, 'Whom do I call educated?' and answers: first, those who handle well the things that meet them each day and possess a good reputation for judging the times so as to aim for the most part at what is beneficial; second, those who conduct themselves toward their associates with propriety and justice, bearing the unpleasantness and heaviness of others easily and lightly, and presenting themselves as lightly and moderately as possible to their companions; third, those who master their pleasures and are not utterly defeated by misfortunes, but behave manfully in them and live worthily of the nature they share; fourth, and most important, those who are not corrupted by good fortune, nor carried out of themselves, nor made arrogant, but remain steadfast in the discipline of sound judgment. He concludes by saying that those who possess a well-ordered soul not merely in one of these respects but in all of them are wise, perfect men who possess every virtue.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological distinctions regarding God's nature (unborn, unneeding, etc.) and the philosophical references. Pass B correctly identifies the Levitical allusion and provides the necessary scripture citation (Leviticus 1:9) for the 'whole burnt offerings' mentioned in the Greek. Pass A is a faithful rendering of the Greek text.
